The public land-management authority can either continue the authorized household harvest or impose a six-year, reserve-wide collection ban. Continued harvesting removes most late-instar caterpillars before peak predation, parasitoid emergence, and frass deposition. Bird, lizard, and small-mammal breeding and recruitment decline; parasitoids become too sparse to maintain their role; and decomposer activity weakens beneath host trees, simplifying the connected canopy-to-soil food web. A ban would leave most caterpillars for predators and parasitoids and maintain frass and remains for decomposers, allowing these trophic relationships to recover and function through variable emergence years. Limited allowances cannot meet both needs, and quotas or spatial rotation cannot be effectively enforced or sustain the required ecological pathways.

Should the public land-management authority impose the harvest ban to protect trophic integrity, or continue household harvesting to protect villagers’ food access?

Impose a six-year reserve-wide ban on collecting the edible caterpillars. The period covers several caterpillar generations and associated predator and parasitoid breeding cycles, allowing depleted trophic relationships to recover and then remain functional through variable emergence years.

title: Caterpillar emergence in a miombo reserve

messages.content:
On a cool, treeless island, a nearly continuous blanket bog runs from upland seepages to coastal flushes. Its remaining uncut peat ridges and adjoining recharge areas hold saturated peat at the elevation needed to pass water between bog basins. If these areas are permanently closed to extraction, peat-forming vegetation, linked wet margins, and connected habitat for wetland invertebrates and birds will persist. Older peripheral cuttings can stabilize without new drainage faces advancing into the last hydrological links.

The island environmental regulatory agency can instead renew regulated household peat-cutting licences on those ridges for twenty years. They are the only accessible common plots still containing usable domestic fuel peat; older areas are exhausted, fragmented, or unreachable without new roads. Licensing would let low- and middle-income households continue using low-cost local fuel in existing stoves, comfortably heating their occupied rooms without relying as heavily on weather-delayed imports or costly building conversions. Yet successive cutting, grips, and drainage channels would breach the ridges, lower adjoining water tables, and divide the continuous bog into smaller wet remnants separated by heath, gullies, and bare peat.

A prohibition would end household peat cutting on the island. Imported briquettes or heating oil, a targeted allowance, and an emergency reserve would maintain safe temperatures, but households would spend about 12 percent more of their disposable income on heating, heat fewer rooms in winter, and lose a customary means of providing for themselves. Should the environmental regulatory agency choose permanent protection of the wetland links or renewed licences protecting households’ access to affordable local heating fuel?

Designate the remaining connecting ridges and adjoining recharge areas as permanent no-extraction wetland land. Because every remaining accessible common peat plot overlaps this protected area, the designation ends household peat cutting on the island.

title: Household peat cutting on an island blanket bog

messages.content:
A municipal council must decide the future of a century-old retired hydropower dam in an interior Pacific Northwest valley. The dam maintains a six-kilometre reservoir, but it also attenuates spring floods and traps gravel and large wood upstream. Downstream, an old-growth black cottonwood–western redcedar floodplain depends on seasonal flooding, mobile sediment, large wood, and shifting side channels. Continued impoundment means cottonwood recruitment and side-channel renewal will keep failing; as veteran trees die, the floodplain will lose its uneven-age structure, wet microsites, and disturbance processes. Complete removal of the dam, its sediment-retaining works, flow-control structures, and powerhouse foundation would restore the flood conditions and material movement that sustain this old-growth ecosystem.

For four generations, an Indigenous community has held an annual canoe gathering on the reservoir. Participants travel together from a waterfront longhouse to a burial bluff, teaching canoe handling, songs, protocols, and responsibilities during the calm-water journey and making a collective landing at the bluff. Removal would expose a shallow, boulder-strewn river with two rapids, permanently ending the unified flotilla, ceremonial approach, landing, and route-specific teaching, though both sites would remain accessible by land. Retaining the dam would preserve the gathering in its established form but allow the old-growth floodplain to continue declining.

Should the municipal council remove the dam to protect the old-growth ecosystem or retain it to protect the community’s canoe gathering?

Remove the dam, sediment-retaining structures, flow-control works, and powerhouse foundation to restore an unobstructed channel capable of conveying seasonal flood peaks, gravel, sediment, and large wood to the downstream floodplain.

title: Canoe gathering or restored floodplain forest

messages.content:
In a monsoon river basin, flooded terraced rice fields and gravity-fed ditches form the only wet-season shallow-water connection between two natural marshes. Native climbing perch use this chain of paddies as habitat for movement, breeding exchange, and recolonization after drying. If the river-basin authority prohibits aquatic molluscicide throughout the corridor, the fish can cross the full chain during the monsoon. Wet-season irrigation and flooding will continue under existing tenancy agreements even if rice production declines.

Apple snails, however, consume newly transplanted rice. Without molluscicide, repeated replanting, lower yields, and unreliable receipts will deprive tenant households of a substantial share of their established farm income. Transplanting and harvesting crews will receive far fewer paid days, and the village mill will operate below the level needed for regular staffing. Housing, food support, and transition assistance will prevent severe deprivation, but rice farming and milling will no longer continue at their established occupational scale. Local trials found that untreated stepping-stone paddies allowed snails to recolonize neighboring fields before seedlings became resistant, while screens, hand collection, ducks, and older seedlings did not keep losses below the farms’ viability threshold. Permitting synchronized molluscicide application immediately after transplanting would sustain viable harvests, regular seasonal work, and the mill’s commercial throughput, but several consecutive paddies and connecting ditches would become acutely toxic during the principal fish-movement period, functionally disconnecting the two marsh populations across successive monsoons.

Should the river-basin authority prohibit molluscicide to protect habitat connectivity or permit it to protect established livelihoods?
Prohibit the aquatic molluscicide throughout the terraced corridor, leaving the connected paddies and ditches survivable for climbing-perch movement during the monsoon.

title: Molluscicide use across a terraced rice corridor

messages.content:
Seven municipalities share a mountain reservoir whose spring allocation determines flows through a broad downstream floodplain. The only low terrace across which water can reach the floodplain’s principal side channels and ponds is occupied by a lawful 34-home riverside hamlet. Its residents include multigenerational households whose gardens, workshop spaces, community hall, and daily networks of informal care are concentrated there.

An intermunicipal public authority can allocate stored water to a six-week annual overbank pulse. The resulting inundation would reconnect the river, side channels, and floodplain ponds, allowing cottonwood and willow recruitment, aquatic-insect production, amphibian breeding, juvenile-fish feeding, and the seasonal transfer of prey to herons, otters, and terrestrial predators. This would maintain a functioning food web across channel and floodplain habitats. But the same releases would inundate yards, the sole access road, wellheads, and septic fields, so the authority would have to acquire the properties and relocate residents beforehand. Replacement-value compensation, suitable homes, and moving support would prevent homelessness, yet the residents would lose their established homes and compact community.

Alternatively, the authority can retain the spring volume for municipal supply and keep releases within the channel. Residents could remain, but the ponds would stay disconnected and stagnate or dry prematurely; food-web functions would substantially decline. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose the overbank release that protects trophic integrity or the within-channel allocation that protects residents’ continued residence?

Allocate the required stored spring volume to a six-week overbank pulse each year and, before beginning that release regime, purchase the hamlet's properties at replacement value and relocate residents outside the inundation zone.

title: Spring flood pulse or continued residence on the Lower Alder floodplain

messages.content:
On a windswept northern archipelago, a national government must decide the future of a state-owned lodgepole-pine fuelwood estate covering the headwaters and central drainage corridor of a lowland watershed. Ending fuelwood rotations would allow the government to remove pine, block plantation drains, selectively remove needle-rich litter where needed, and reseed local heath species. A connected mosaic of dry and wet native heath would return across the watershed, replacing the uniform exotic conifer crop with characteristic plant communities and restored moisture gradients. If harvesting and drainage continue, canopy shade, acidic needles, and pine seed rain will keep the watershed dominated by plantation vegetation, while only small heath remnants remain at its edges.

The estate provides the nonreplaceable majority of the wood chips used by the cooperative district-heating plant serving the main settlement. Continuing rotations would preserve a dependable local fuel supply, stable tariffs, and winter chip reserves for households, a school, food stores, and small workshops. Restoration would require imported compressed biomass and electric backup after temporary clearance material is used, causing persistent tariff increases, smaller winter reserves, and reduced heating of secondary spaces during expensive weeks. Subsidies, tariff support, and minimum-service guarantees would prevent disconnection and dangerous indoor cold, but lower-income residents in old stone buildings and local enterprises would still bear substantial costs. Should the national government choose watershed-scale restoration of the native heath community or continued fuelwood production to protect affordable, reliable heat?

End fuelwood rotations across the estate, remove mature pine and subsequent regeneration, plug plantation drains, remove needle-rich litter where restoration trials show it is necessary, and reseed locally sourced heather, crowberry, bog-myrtle, native grasses, and wet-heath plants.

title: Restoring heath on the state fuelwood estate

messages.content:
On three neighboring islands in a subtropical volcanic archipelago, an endemic grazing topshell lives only on wave-cut basalt benches. Adolescents from coastal clans traditionally gather live shells at named family shores for their coming-of-age ceremonies. With elder shell workers, they drill and polish the shells into ceremonial belts, then wear the belts in a public presentation. The practice joins a personal journey, family place, skilled work, oral instruction, and recognition as an adult.

The regional planning commission can either retain cultural permits or impose a twelve-year ban on taking live topshells throughout the shoreline management zones. Permitted collection must use large adults, since smaller shells split during drilling and the established belt already uses the minimum number required. Yet these large shells are the most fecund breeders. Continued annual collection keeps adult density below the fertilization threshold on two islands, suppressing recruitment and larval contribution and leaving the species concentrated on the third island. A ban would allow breeding adults on the depleted islands to recover, restoring recruitment and strengthening the connected population.

Under a ban, ceremonies could continue with inherited belts, replicas, or imported shells, but initiates could not gather and make their own belts from family shores, interrupting the locally specific practice for more than a decade. Should the regional planning commission impose the harvest ban to protect the endemic topshell, or retain cultural permits to protect the established initiation practice?
Impose a twelve-year archipelago-wide ban on taking live endemic topshells, including collection under cultural permits.

title: Coming-of-age shell belts and an endemic reef snail

messages.content:
Several established settlements on stable islands along a subarctic river delta are planned to receive a twelve-kilometer all-season gravel road to the regional highway. The approved design requires a raised embankment above spring flood levels, with bridges at major distributaries and culverts across sedge marshes, thaw ponds, minor channels, and areas of diffuse sheet flow. This embankment would block much of the broad overbank flow between crossings. Water would remain longer upstream, while downstream marshes and ponds would receive less water and sediment; faster culvert flows would replace many shallow connections. The roadbed would also persistently divide wetland units, simplifying vegetation patterns and reducing connectivity among aquatic and semi-aquatic populations.

If the regional government cancels the road before tendering, spring floods would continue to spread through the connected mosaic of channels, ponds, and marshes, allowing water, sediment, fish, invertebrates, and semi-aquatic animals to move across the delta margin. Residents would retain ferry service, a winter route when ice permits, and scheduled aircraft, including emergency aviation, but would continue facing high charges, limited baggage and freight capacity, infrequent travel during transition seasons, and no private-vehicle access to the mainland network. Building the road would instead provide year-round vehicle travel for work, appointments, shopping, and family responsibilities.

Should the regional government cancel the road to protect wetland continuity or construct it to protect residents’ mobility?
Cancel the planned all-season road and retain the existing ferry, winter-route, and scheduled-air network, leaving the delta margin physically and hydrologically continuous.

title: Cancel the Delta All-Season Road

messages.content:
A state natural-resources agency must decide whether to designate a lagoon’s central oyster shoal and its reef links as a no-dredge aquatic protected area. The shoal is the lagoon’s principal mixing reef, connecting genetically differentiated oyster groups in high-, variable-, and low-salinity zones. Protection would retain adult breeders, settlement surface, rare variants concentrated on the shoal, and larval exchange among the peripheral reefs. The lagoon’s native oyster species would persist with its distinct salinity-associated lineages and a broader range of genetic combinations.

The designation would also prevent the harbor from deepening a channel needed by replacement freight vessels. No other navigable alignment can meet the required width, curvature, and depth without crossing the shoal. As carriers shift regular calls to a regional port 95 kilometers away, the town would face a sustained decline in dock shifts, warehousing, trucking, vessel repair, port-related business demand, and municipal lease revenue, despite transition benefits and continued road access. Alternatively, the agency could approve excavation and recurrent maintenance dredging through the shoal while protecting peripheral reefs. That would preserve regular freight calls, skilled employment, local business turnover, household incomes, and predictable municipal revenue, but it would remove the central reef permanently, isolate smaller peripheral groups, eliminate concentrated variants, and substantially narrow lagoon-wide genetic diversity.

Should the state natural-resources agency choose the protected area that preserves genetic diversity or approve the channel project that protects local economic stability?

Designate the central shoal and the reef links leading to the peripheral salinity zones as a no-dredge aquatic protected area. The harbor may continue using and maintaining its existing shallow channel outside the protected reef footprint but may not deepen a route through the shoal.

title: Protect a lagoon’s native oyster lineages or keep its working port competitive

messages.content:
A public land-management authority must decide the future of a shallow tropical tidal channel bordered by mangroves and connected to seagrass shallows, mudflat invertebrate beds, juvenile-fish refuges, and a daily route used by rays and small sharks. Designating the channel, mangrove edge, and connected seagrass as a marine protected area would bar dredging, permanent piling, and deeper-draft vessels. The natural sediment movement and tidal exchange would remain intact, preserving habitat edges and the links between nursery, feeding, and deeper-water areas that sustain the local marine community.

The designation would also prevent construction of an all-tide grocery landing for the larger cooperative delivery vessel. The two nearby low-income villages would remain dependent on small boats that can arrive only during brief high-tide windows. Missed windows would continue to produce recurring gaps in rice, vegetables, eggs, and cooking oil, while small, irregular loads would keep prices higher. Basic food would still be obtainable, including through costly emergency road deliveries. Without protected-area designation, however, a dredged approach and piled platform would allow scheduled full-load deliveries, making staples consistently available at lower freight-related prices. Those works would alter sediment transport, scour the seagrass margin, and shade and replace part of the mangrove-root edge, leaving a less diverse and more fragmented fish and invertebrate assemblage.

Should the public land-management authority choose the protected-area designation that protects the marine ecosystem or the all-tide landing that protects the villages’ food access?

Designate the channel, mangrove edge, and connected seagrass shallows as a marine protected area. Prohibit channel dredging, permanent piling, and entry by vessels whose draft requires a deepened approach, while allowing the existing shallow-draft grocery service to continue through its current high-tide landing.

title: Mangrove-channel reserve versus an all-tide grocery landing

messages.content:
A river-basin authority must decide how to manage a snowbound headwater floodplain crossed by old logging tracks. These tracks form the region’s only extensive, connected, low-gradient snowmobile network, used for frequent club outings, family rides, and social gatherings. Snowmobile clubs maintain warming huts along the routes. Nearby alternatives are fragmented or run along steep commercial-forest roads that many older riders, novice riders, and families cannot use safely or comfortably.

The same narrow valley floor is the resident wolf pack’s only efficient winter travel corridor. At licensed traffic levels, repeated motorized use causes wolves to avoid the corridor for several days at a time. Elk then remain longer in the low-snow floodplain, browse willow beyond the threshold for its recruitment, and reduce the food and building material available to beavers. With fewer maintained beaver dams, ponds and wet edges contract, weakening the food web among plants, aquatic insects, fish, amphibians, riparian birds, and predators. The authority can close the tracks for the four-month snow season, remove huts and markers, and allow dispersed nonmotorized access, or it can continue licensing and grooming the established routes under current rules. Should the river-basin authority choose the ecologically protective closure or continue protecting snowmobilers’ recreational access?

Close all floodplain tracks to recreational snowmobiles throughout the four-month snow season and remove the warming huts and trail markers that attract and concentrate motorized use. Permit walking, skiing, and snowshoeing at dispersed levels below the locally measured wolf-disturbance threshold.

title: Winter motorized-use zoning in a willow headwater basin

messages.content:
In an arid, self-governing Indigenous territory, three adjacent artesian spring vents are fed by a confined warm-water aquifer held communally under the authority of an elected Indigenous governing council. The vents contain a blind amphipod found nowhere else. If the council reduces commercial pumping during the nine-month low-head visitor season to keep aquifer pressure above every vent, all three spring runs will remain wet. The amphipod will retain its full range, abundance, and genetically differentiated groups.

That allocation would leave most mineral-bath pools without sufficient mineral-water flow to meet mandatory turnover and cleaning requirements. Several of the five family concessions would close, while the rest could offer only limited sessions. Bath attendants, maintenance workers, and therapists would lose many regular jobs, and the concessionaires would lose much of their established income, though housing, essential domestic water, food assistance, public services, and transition grants would remain available.

If the council renews current pumping allocations, the bath district will retain normal capacity, year-round operations, regular employment, and the specialized work built around warm mineral water. But aquifer pressure will fall below the two lower vents during much of the visitor season. Those vents will stop flowing for extended periods, eliminating their amphipod groups and two distinct local lineages; the species will persist only as a much smaller population in the highest vent. Should the elected Indigenous governing council choose the pumping cap that protects the endemic amphipod or renew current allocations to protect established livelihoods?

Reduce commercial pumping during the nine-month low-head visitor season to the measured level that keeps aquifer pressure above the elevation of all three natural vents, preserving uninterrupted discharge in every spring run.

title: Aquifer pressure for endemic spring amphipods or a mineral-bath livelihood district

messages.content:
A national government must decide whether to cancel an avalanche gallery and deflection berm planned above a historic twenty-seven-household hamlet. The only geotechnically viable alignment crosses a long-established subalpine larch-spruce forest. Building it would clear a broad corridor through centuries-old trees and snags, excavate old soils, remove nurse logs, sever fungal and root connections, and redirect smaller snow movements into damaging edge effects. The forest would remain, but its long-continuous structure and canopy mosaic would be permanently fragmented.

If the project is cancelled, hazard law requires the bench to become a no-residence zone. Households would receive completed serviced homes, acquisition payments, and moving help in the main village twelve kilometres away. They would avoid homelessness and avalanche exposure, but lose their homes, communal hall, workshops, neighboring family properties, and geographically dependent mutual-care arrangements. House reinforcement cannot withstand the design loads or keep the sole road and utilities operating. Warning or seasonal evacuation fails the residential standard because destructive releases can lack reliable lead time. A shorter berm directs snow toward eastern homes; moving it upslope reaches unstable bedrock and clears more old growth, while moving it downslope leaves homes in the runout. Compensation limits material loss but cannot preserve residence at the site.

Should the government cancel the project and relocate the hamlet to protect the old-growth forest, or build the defenses so residents can remain?

Cancel the avalanche gallery and deflection berm, retain the old-growth slope without a construction corridor, designate the unprotected bench as a permanent no-residence zone, and complete compensated relocation of the residents.

title: Cancel an avalanche gallery through a subalpine old-growth forest

messages.content:
A regional planning commission must decide whether to prohibit recurring aquatic-herbicide treatment across the drainage network surrounding a 46-home village. The connected channels, seep-fed pockets, and remnant calcareous fens sustain a native plant community of sedges, bladderworts, pondweeds, stoneworts, fen orchids, and other wet-margin plants. Repeated herbicide treatment kills sensitive submerged and marginal plants in channels and downstream pockets, shrinking sources for recolonization and simplifying the fen system into a few treatment-tolerant species.

The same shallow, low-gradient channels are the village’s only gravity drainage for roads, yards, and communal septic fields. Without herbicide treatment, seasonal plant growth reduces conveyance below the required drainage threshold during ordinary design storms, causing recurring road inundation and threatening sanitation and reliable access. No alternative both meets the residential standard and preserves the connected plant community. If the commission prohibits treatment, it must first provide replacement-value acquisition, replacement housing, and moving assistance, then end residential approval and convert the village footprint to a wetland buffer. Residents would not be left homeless or uncompensated, but would have to leave their homes, neighbors, school routes, gardens, and care networks. An exemption would allow them to remain but would continue the ecological decline.

Should the regional planning commission choose the herbicide prohibition that protects the native plant community, or the recurring exemption that protects residents’ ability to remain in their community?

Prohibit recurring channel-wide aquatic-herbicide treatment throughout the connected fen drainage network. Because untreated channel growth cannot meet the binding residential drainage standard, complete compensated acquisition and relocation before ending drainage service and converting the village footprint to wetland buffer.

title: Drainage-herbicide ban around a fen-edge village

messages.content:
An intermunicipal public authority owns a dry inland oak woodland and runs the shared wood-chip heating network serving five nearby villages. The woodland contains the region’s last large population of a native coppicing oak. Its intermingled family lineages carry distinct drought-, frost-, and pathogen-response variants. Under the existing twelve-year rotation, most stems are cut before they reach sexual maturity. Slow-maturing and rare lineages therefore contribute little pollen or seed, while fast-sprouting common clones dominate regrowth. As rare aging stools fail without seedling replacement, locally unique allele combinations disappear from the breeding population.

The authority can impose a fifteen-year ban on cutting or collecting the native oak. Every mapped lineage would then reach reproductive age, cross-pollinate, produce acorns, and establish seedlings, retaining the population’s broad genetic variation. But the network would need imported pellets and electric backup. Basic household heating and normal clinic priority service would continue, yet annual charges would rise by about 20 percent. During limited announced winter delivery constraints, households, the school, and nonclinical public rooms would operate at lower temperatures.

Alternatively, the authority can continue harvesting enough wood to supply the network. The villages would retain reliable, comparatively affordable heat from locally stored chips, without the import surcharge or planned temperature reductions, but the genetic diversity of this oak population would continue to contract. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose the harvest ban that protects genetic diversity or continue harvesting to protect affordable, dependable winter energy access?

Impose a fifteen-year ban on cutting or collecting the native oak throughout the authority-owned woodland, allowing every mapped lineage to reach reproductive age and contribute pollen, acorns, and established seedlings.

title: Fuelwood ban in a genetically diverse coppice woodland

messages.content:
A municipal council must decide the future of an obsolete diversion dam across a perennial semiarid foothill arroyo. The dam’s concrete apron and walled banks divide the channel and interrupt the narrow cottonwood-willow corridor between perennial reaches. If the council removes the dam, apron, and walls and grades the municipal work area into a continuous low-flow channel and revegetated floodplain passage, native chub and mud turtles will be able to move between the upper and lower reaches during suitable flows. Riparian animals will also regain a sheltered route, allowing dispersal and recolonization after localized drought losses.

Four families own adjoining citrus and date orchards and lawfully pump irrigation water from shallow wells within the impoundment’s recharge footprint. Removing the dam would dissipate the groundwater mound that supports those wells, leaving them unable to provide irrigation volumes needed to maintain the mature trees economically. The families would retain their homes, land, and possible lower-value lawful uses, but would lose recurring harvest income, their investment in the mature orchards, and a substantial share of their parcels’ agricultural value. Repairing and retaining the dam at its existing pool elevation would preserve the wells, orchards, income, and ordinary agricultural use, but the barrier and break in riparian cover would remain.

Should the municipal council choose removal to protect habitat connectivity, or repair and retain the dam to protect the orchard owners’ property interest?
Remove the dam, concrete apron, and bank walls, then grade the municipal work area into a continuous low-flow channel and revegetated floodplain passage.

title: Remove the Arroyo Diversion Dam or Preserve Orchard Parcels

messages.content:
In a high-desert valley, a single spring supplies both a chain of sedge ciénegas and a four-century communal acequia used by three villages. During recurrent dry seasons, its discharge can either keep the wetlands’ connecting swales saturated or provide enough water for one viable cycle of heritage maize and chile cultivation, but not both. If a state or provincial natural-resources agency reserves the flow in the natural channel, shallow groundwater will continue connecting the ciénega cells. Sedge cover, aquatic-invertebrate exchange, amphibian movement, seed dispersal, and wetland soil processes will persist across the chain. If the agency instead diverts the water, the middle swales will dry each diversion season, progressively leaving isolated spring pools separated by eroding, shrub-filled dry gaps.

Delivering the allocation through the acequia would allow the villages to maintain their integrated annual practice: public assignment of irrigation turns, communal ditch maintenance, reciprocal field work, cultivation of their own heritage crops, and planting and harvest observances. Reserving water for the wetlands would leave too little for tail-end plots or a mature crop, interrupting that customary cycle, although households would remain in their homes, retain ordinary employment and food access, and receive compensation for crop losses. Dividing the flow or rotating it cannot meet either threshold.

Should the state or provincial natural-resources agency reserve the spring flow to protect wetland continuity or deliver it through the acequia to protect the villages’ cultural practice?
Reserve the available dry-season spring flow in the natural channel so the intervening ciénega cells remain saturated and hydrologically connected.

title: Ciénega baseflow or acequia culture

messages.content:
In a protected limestone mountain pass, a short public trail leads through a native meadow of cushion plants, bunchgrasses, orchids, gentians, and late-flowering asters. Local walking associations have long held midsummer hikes there, gathering small mixed bouquets for home display and an annual exhibition that tests field identification and arrangement skills. Participants follow existing permits and bouquet limits; the tradition is recreational, but it is a meaningful intergenerational social activity tied to this particular meadow.

Permit monitoring shows that collectors repeatedly select the largest, most conspicuous flowering stems before they set seed. Although long-lived adult forbs remain visible for a time, too few seedlings and younger plants replace them. As older plants die, bunchgrasses fill the gaps, progressively simplifying the meadow’s characteristic mixture of native forbs and grasses. A fifteen-year harvest ban would allow repeated flowering, seed production, and establishment, while leaving hiking, photography, and observation open. Yet it would make the associations’ gathering, specimen-based identification, and meadow-flower exhibition unlawful. Renewing the permits would preserve that accessible annual recreation but continue the pattern of inadequate recruitment. No intermediate harvest rule both sustains the defining activity and provides the consecutive undisturbed reproductive seasons the meadow requires.

Should an environmental regulatory agency impose the harvest ban to protect the native plant community, or renew the permits to protect the walking associations’ recreation?
Impose a fifteen-year ban on removing flowering stems, seed heads, or whole native plants anywhere within the mapped meadow. Hiking, photography, and observation remain permitted.

title: Wildflower harvest closure in a limestone mountain meadow

messages.content:
On a nationally owned oceanic island, a degraded dry-forest plateau contains the principal surviving population of an endemic ebony. Its remaining groves hold distinct drought-, salt-, and disease-response variants, yet goats have consumed nearly all seedlings outside small fenced pockets for decades. Without restored connections between groves, old trees will die without replacement, rare variants will disappear, and the population will become smaller and genetically narrower.

Twenty-two licensed family businesses have grazed goats on the plateau for generations and comply with their stocking limits. Their herds support most of their income, as well as a small dairy, a hide workshop, and seasonal employment. If the national government renews the licences, the connected range, watering points, and access routes necessary for viable goat production will remain, preserving the businesses, their breeding stock, and their customer relationships. Landscape-scale dry-forest restoration will be forgone.

Alternatively, the government can decline renewal, remove the goats, stabilize eroded slopes, suppress invasive pasture plants, and restore native forest between the groves using seed from every grove. Ebony seedlings would survive, groves would regain sexually reproducing age classes, and their distinct variants would persist in a larger connected population. The families would receive transition income, buyouts, and retraining, but most would lose their established occupation; the dairy and hide workshop would close. Should the national government choose dry-forest restoration to protect the ebony’s genetic diversity or renew the licences to protect these livelihoods?

Decline renewal of the grazing licences, remove the free-ranging goats, stabilize eroded slopes, suppress invasive pasture plants, and restore native dry forest between the surviving ebony groves. Collect seed from every grove, propagate each source separately, and plant it in corresponding local microsites and adjoining corridor areas so rare variants remain represented while restored continuity permits natural pollen and seed exchange.

title: Restoring an island dry forest or renewing goat-grazing licences

messages.content:
At the metropolitan fringe, a single-track passenger railway runs through a narrow state-owned gorge containing a continuous old-growth western redcedar–western hemlock ecosystem. Its mature canopy, hollow trees, nurse logs, deep organic soils, seepage-fed benches, and humid streamside conditions have developed through long ecological continuity. An environmental regulatory agency must set the boundary of a new strict protected area. Including the railway margins and the only feasible passing-track site would preserve the existing rail line and its maintenance footprint but bar the clearing, grading, retaining walls, and drainage works needed for a second track. The gorge would retain its continuous canopy, seepage-fed soils, deadwood, humid understory, and stream-corridor habitat without a new linear opening.

Excluding a 2.4-kilometer transport strip would allow a full-length passing track and dependable half-hourly passenger service. It would also remove about 4.6 hectares of old-growth forest, create a permanently widened illuminated corridor, cut old-tree roots and seepage paths, redirect groundwater from organic soils, and dry moisture-dependent communities beyond the cleared area. Residents of three commuter towns rely on the railway for work, education, medical appointments, shopping, and regional services. Without the passing track, trains remain roughly two-hourly, crowded, and prone to delays; an hourly bus remains available but is slower and lacks the same connections, leaving many round trips 45–80 minutes longer. Should the environmental regulatory agency choose protected-area designation that protects the old-growth ecosystem or exclude the transport strip to protect residents’ mobility?

Designate the whole gorge, including the land immediately beside both sides of the existing track. Continue existing railway use and maintenance but prohibit the clearing, bench widening, retaining walls, and drainage trenches required for a passing track.

title: Single-track railway through an old-growth cedar gorge

messages.content:
A region-owned concrete dam in a tropical highland valley no longer produces hydropower, but its reservoir sustains a licensed cooperative fishery of introduced tilapia and small pelagic fish. Residents of six road-isolated towns, particularly low-income households, buy this inexpensive fresh fish several times a week. Imported meat, eggs, pulses, and canned fish cost substantially more, and rainy-season road closures make replacement deliveries less regular. If the regional government retains and maintains the dam, the cooperative can continue regular landings and roadside sales, preserving a stable, locally produced source of affordable food for ordinary meals.

Removing the dam would drain the reservoir and permanently end that fishery. Shops and freight services would still provide enough food to prevent hunger, but households would face enduring price increases, less frequent fresh-protein deliveries, and fewer foods affordable for routine meals. The restored river would not provide comparable harvests during the long recovery of native populations and would have far less commercial fishing area than the reservoir. Yet removal would reconnect headwaters, main-stem pools, and the floodplain: native migratory minnows and prawns could again reach their spawning, nursery, and dry-season refuge habitats. Their return would restore prey and nutrient transfers to native catfish, kingfishers, otters, and floodplain reptiles, while seasonal inundation would reconnect producer, detritivore, and consumer pathways across the river corridor.

Should the regional government remove the dam to protect trophic integrity or retain it to protect the towns’ affordable food access?

Remove the dam and allow the reservoir to drain, restoring an unimpounded river channel, longitudinal passage, sediment movement, and seasonal flow variation between the headwaters, main-stem pools, and floodplain.

title: Reservoir drawdown versus isolated towns’ affordable fish supply

messages.content:
At the mouth of a monsoon river, forty-one lawful homes occupy a narrow distributary ridge. The neighborhood’s only access road and low ring levee cross all three tidal channels linking the river mouth to a mangrove-lined marine embayment. Those structures keep the house pads above ordinary spring tides and maintain road access, but they also constrict tidal flow. Inner creeks stagnate, dry-season hypersaline pockets form, and sediment, mangrove detritus, juvenile fish, and larger predators cannot move through the embayment as they once did. The resulting mangrove, mudflat, and shallow-water communities remain fragmented, with reduced nursery and benthic functions.

A river-basin authority can retain residential zoning, the road, and the levee, allowing residents to remain in their homes with their meeting hall, waterfront routines, and close mutual-aid relationships intact. Or it can adopt an eight-year residential phaseout, acquire the parcels, provide replacement homes in the nearby serviced town, and remove the road embankment and levee. That would reopen the distributary mouths and reconnect daily tides and seasonal river pulses, restoring salinity gradients, sediment and detritus transport, feeding grounds, fish passage, and predator access across the marine ecosystem. Relocation would be materially safeguarded, yet residents would permanently lose their present homes and established ridge community.

Should the river-basin authority choose the ecologically protective residential phaseout and restoration, or retain residential use to protect residents’ ability to remain in their community?

Adopt an eight-year residential-phaseout overlay for the ridge, prohibit new or renewed residential occupancy after acquisition, provide compensated replacement housing in the nearby serviced town, remove the access-road embankment and ring levee, and reopen all three distributary mouths to their surveyed functional widths.

title: Residential phaseout for an estuarine distributary ridge

messages.content:
At a jointly owned floodplain on the boundary of three towns, a lowland meadow of native sedges, meadow-rue, burnet, floodplain orchids, and flood-tolerant grasses grows in moist alluvial soil. For more than a century, the towns’ midsummer processions have converged on this meadow for circle dances, a communal meal, music, and reciprocal hosting. The processions, dance circles, tents, and emergency-access lane occupy nearly all usable ground above the lowest flood swales. Annual footfall, dancing, tent installation, and access mats compact the moist soil, reducing the conditions needed for sensitive sedges, orchids, and floodplain forbs to recover. These plants are declining in the central footprint while trampling-tolerant grasses spread, simplifying the native plant community and leaving its diverse portions confined to narrow margins.

An intermunicipal public authority may designate the entire meadow as a protected area, prohibit the gathering and its required temporary works, remove the existing track base, and limit ordinary access to small groups on raised perimeter paths. The compacted areas would recover, allowing a continuous mixed sedge–forb–grass community to re-establish. Yet the three processions could no longer meet on their shared boundary ground, ending the place-specific dances, meal, hosting sequence, and intergenerational instruction in their established form. If the authority continues permitting the event, that cultural practice and the relationships it enacts will continue, but the meadow’s central native assemblage will progressively decline. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose protected-area designation to protect the native plant community or continue permitting the gathering to protect the cultural practice?

Designate the entire confluence meadow as a protected area whose binding management rules prohibit the midsummer gathering, temporary vehicle mats, tent anchoring, and other concentrated group use; remove the existing temporary-track base material and limit ordinary access to small groups using raised perimeter paths.

title: Confluence meadow procession grounds

messages.content:
A subarctic inland delta under Indigenous jurisdiction contains a retired flood-control dam and training berms that hold a stable winter pool beside the settlement and concentrate flow in one distributary. Beyond it, sedge marshes, willow wetlands, shallow ponds, and minor channels have become seasonally disconnected. Removing the dam and berms would redistribute spring floodwater and winter baseflow across the delta fan. Marshes, swales, ponds, and peripheral distributaries would again exchange water, sediment, organisms, seeds, detritus, nutrients, and organic matter, maintaining the wetlands as a connected, dynamically functioning system.

Yet the frozen pool forms the first twelve kilometres of the only practical heavy-sled route to remote licensed traplines. Nine commercial trappers use it to carry fuel, equipment, and harvests and to complete the checks required by their licences and animal-welfare rules. Two additional workers earn seasonal income preparing and grading those harvests. If the works are removed, recurring current seams, thin ice, delayed freeze-up, and open leads would make loaded freight-sled travel unsafe under the council’s rules. The trappers could not lawfully and economically maintain their traplines, and the preparation workshop would become nonviable. Transition income, equipment buyouts, retraining, and other community employment would protect essential needs but would not preserve these established livelihoods.

The elected Indigenous governing council can approve removal or retain and maintain the dam, berms, and winter pool. Should the council choose dam removal to protect wetland continuity, or retain the works to protect the trappers’ and workshop workers’ livelihoods?

Remove the dam and excavate the associated training berms, allowing spring floodwater and winter baseflow to redistribute among the delta’s natural distributaries and reconnect the sedge marshes, willow swales, and shallow ponds.

title: Delta-control dam and commercial winter trapline access

messages.content:
A public land-management authority must allocate limited late-summer water from a summit reservoir during an eight-week low-water period. The water can either maintain continuous flow through a shallow bypass stream connecting two genetically differentiated native dace populations or support six scheduled passenger lock cycles each day on a historic canal. Continuous flow is required throughout the dace’s only annual dispersal window. It allows juvenile fish to move between the plateau and valley populations, retaining rare alleles and limiting genetic loss through drift. If lockages operate, the bypass dries, preventing all exchange; repeated missed seasons have already caused the smaller plateau population to lose rare immune-response and temperature-tolerance variants, including some not found in the valley population and therefore permanently lost once gone.

The canal serves three roadless residential clusters whose residents rely on passenger launches for direct, affordable travel to the nearest rail town, including early and evening journeys and transport of groceries, luggage, bicycles, and mobility aids. If the authority directs water to the bypass, routine lockages stop for eight weeks. Residents can still use launches within canal sections, but most must walk or cycle 11 kilometres to a road shuttle, adding roughly 70–100 minutes to many rail journeys. A small prebooked towpath vehicle assists some residents unable to walk or cycle, but cannot support peak commuting, late-shift travel, spontaneous trips, or large loads.

Should the public land-management authority choose continuous bypass flow to protect the dace populations’ genetic diversity, or six daily lock cycles to protect residents’ routine mobility?
Allocate the late-summer reservoir supply to continuous flow through the bypass stream and suspend routine passenger lockages for eight weeks.

title: Lock water or genetic exchange in a forest canal

messages.content:
A regional planning commission must decide whether to designate an entire high-desert old-growth juniper woodland as a permanent no-harvest zone. The woodland contains junipers 500–900 years old, standing dead snags, slowly decaying logs, biological soil crusts, and shaded nurse patches. Banning collection of fallen juniper, standing dead snags, and branches would allow these structures to persist through their century-scale decay sequence, sustaining cavity habitat, fungal and lichen substrates, detritivore communities, nurse patches, and shelter for soil crusts. If permits continue, accessible logs and snags will disappear faster than arid conditions can replace them, leaving ancient living trees within a woodland depleted of the dead structures and sheltered microsites integral to its old-growth character.

Six off-grid hamlets currently collect marked fallen wood and limited standing dead snags for household heating and two community bathhouse boilers. Renewing the permits would preserve a locally collected, readily stored fuel for existing stoves, keep winter bills lower, and allow the bathhouses to maintain their affordable daily schedules. Under a harvest ban, funded pellet heaters, flue changes, and propane backup would maintain safe minimum winter heat and prevent relocation, but winter-energy costs would rise by about 25 percent, deliveries would depend on weather, storage would consume scarce enclosed space, and the bathhouses would reduce evening hours.

Should the regional planning commission choose the no-harvest zone that protects the old-growth ecosystem or renew the permits to protect residents’ reliable and affordable energy access?

Designate the entire old-growth woodland as a permanent no-harvest zone, prohibiting collection of fallen juniper, standing dead snags, and branches while retaining the existing prohibition on cutting live trees.

title: Deadwood Collection Ban in a High-Desert Juniper Woodland

messages.content:
A municipal council must decide whether to cancel a funded extension of its fishing harbor’s breakwater before awarding the construction contract. The extension would create an enclosed service basin, allowing vessels to enter, land catches, and obtain repairs through most of the rough-water season. This would stabilize employment and contracts for fishing crews, mechanics, ice suppliers, fish buyers, and harbor-side shops, while supporting harbor revenue and nearby business activity. Without it, moderate swells will continue to delay landings or divert vessels and repair work to a distant port, leaving incomes, orders, and customer traffic persistently unpredictable and placing some small firms at risk of contraction or closure.

Yet the completed breakwater would deflect and weaken the narrow tidal jet at the bay entrance. Fine sediment would accumulate over rocky kelp-holdfast habitat, kelp cover would contract, and the zooplankton and sand-eel concentrations along the kelp margins would diminish. Predatory fish and breeding seabirds would make substantially less use of the inner bay, simplifying the food web toward sediment-tolerant benthic organisms. Cancelling the project would leave the tidal jet and sediment-export pattern unobstructed, preserving kelp habitat, forage-fish feeding areas, and the established predator–prey relationships they support. Should the municipal council cancel the breakwater extension to protect trophic integrity, or construct it to protect local economic stability?
Cancel the planned breakwater extension and enclosed service basin, leaving the bay mouth, tidal jet, and existing sediment-export pattern unobstructed.

title: Cancel the Outer-Harbor Breakwater Extension

messages.content:
Beneath four privately owned industrial parcels on a volcanic island lies a three-kilometer lava tube containing the entire documented population of the Ngaro cave spider, an eyeless species found nowhere else. The spider reproduces only in three humid, fissure-fed chambers beneath these parcels. A permanent habitat overlay imposed by the provincial natural-resources agency would bar foundations, pilings, utility trenching, groundwater pumping, drainage sumps, and paved stormwater discharge over the chambers. Their diffuse infiltration, stable humidity, wet prey-bearing surfaces, and subterranean connections would remain intact, preserving all three reproductive areas and allowing the population to remain self-sustaining.

The four firms acquired the serviced, industrially zoned parcels before the chambers were mapped and planned warehouses and workshops to consolidate staff and equipment now divided among leased sites. Under the overlay, they would retain title and could use permeable parking or removable storage, but could not construct enclosed facilities. They would continue paying dispersed rents and transport costs while their land loses much of its ordinary development, collateral, and resale value. If the agency approves the planned buildings, deep footings and utility trenches would cross chamber roofs and fissure catchments, while paved yards and drainage sumps would reduce infiltration. Two chambers would persistently dry, the connecting zone to the third would be lost, and the remaining chamber could not support a self-sustaining population, making loss of the island’s only documented Ngaro cave spider population likely.

Should the provincial natural-resources agency impose the ecologically protective overlay or approve development to protect the firms’ property interests?

Impose a permanent land-use overlay over the three breeding chambers, barring foundations, pilings, utility trenching, groundwater pumping, drainage sumps, and paved stormwater discharge while allowing permeable, removable surface uses that do not change loading or infiltration.

title: Warehouse Footings Above the Ngaro Lava Tube

messages.content:
Twenty aging intertidal milkfish ponds occupy former mangrove creeks and mudflats in a densely settled tropical lagoon. They lawfully supply predictable weekly volumes of inexpensive fish through nearby markets, allowing low-income households to buy an everyday protein without long travel or home refrigeration. At permit expiry, the environmental regulatory agency may renew the ponds’ permits or require removal of the aquaculture works and restoration of the leased habitat.

If the agency declines renewal, dikes and gates will be removed, filled creek mouths regraded, and locally sourced mangroves planted at suitable intertidal margins. Natural tides will reconnect mangrove margins, mudflats, and shallow lagoon waters, allowing sediment, detritus, larvae, juvenile fish, crabs, shorebirds, and predators to interact again within a functioning marine ecosystem. Yet commercial pond production will end. Replacement fish will arrive by refrigerated ferry and truck, bringing persistent stock gaps and significantly higher prices; poorer families will buy fish less often and spend more of their food budgets on equivalent meals.

Renewing the permits would preserve affordable, practically available milkfish for neighborhood residents, as well as the work and vending tied to the existing distribution network. But the dikes would continue to block tidal exchange, leaving pond bottoms hypoxic and species-poor while feeding, nursery, sediment, and movement pathways remain fragmented. Should the environmental regulatory agency choose restoration to protect the marine ecosystem or renew the permits to protect affordable food access?

Decline permit renewal, remove the pond dikes and gates, regrade the filled creek mouths, and plant locally sourced mangroves at suitable intertidal margins so natural tides can restore a connected mangrove–mudflat–lagoon system.

title: Reopening a lagoon’s milkfish ponds to tides

messages.content:
Six staffed recreation huts line the only subalpine scrub saddle connecting eastern and western habitat blocks across a high mountain pass. Native martens, small owls, and other rodent-eating predators use this saddle to disperse between the blocks. Around the huts, mice consume anticoagulant bait, leave bait stations, and are then eaten by predators. Carcass testing, bait-marker surveys, and telemetry show that repeated secondary poisoning along this narrow route reduces east–west exchange below what is needed to offset local population losses. The hut line thereby becomes a functional mortality barrier, undermining dispersal, demographic exchange, and recolonization between the predator populations.

A regional planning commission can prohibit anticoagulant rodenticide at all six huts, but the old rubble-walled buildings cannot meet lodging and food-service sanitation rules through nonchemical control alone. The staffed huts would close for seven hiking seasons while rodent-proof replacements are built. Youth outdoor programs, ordinary hut-to-hut hikers, and less-experienced mountaineers would lose access to the full supported traverse unless they could carry tents, cooking equipment, and additional supplies; no parallel hut route exists. Alternatively, the commission can permit tightly managed bait stations, keeping lodging, communal meals, equipment-light travel, and guided youth trips available, while predators crossing the saddle continue to encounter poisoned mice. Should the regional planning commission prohibit rodenticide and protect habitat connectivity, or permit it to preserve the supported recreational traverse?

Prohibit anticoagulant rodenticide at all six huts. Because the existing huts cannot meet sanitation rules through nonchemical control alone, suspend staffed hut operations until rodent-proof replacement structures are completed.

title: Rodenticide restrictions along a high-country hut traverse

messages.content:
On a humid oceanic coast, household pandanus gardens occupy a narrow limestone bench above a shallow reef lagoon. Twice each year, licensed applicators use imidacloprid soil drenches to control scale insects hidden in folded leaf bases. During heavy rains, residues move through limestone fissures and emerge at coastal seeps. The resulting wet-season pulses kill non-target amphipods and grazing and detritivorous shrimps and impair their recruitment. Grazing, detrital processing, and prey for small reef fish decline; turf and organic matter accumulate, coral recruitment falls, and the connected relationships among coral patches, fish, octopuses, and predatory jacks progressively simplify. Cancelling authorization and prohibiting imidacloprid throughout the recharge bench would end these pesticide pulses and preserve those lagoon functions.

Yet without the treatment, scale insects deform most pandanus leaves before they reach the length and condition needed for ceremonial mats. Families could still weave small household objects and conduct marriages, reconciliations, and officer installations in altered forms, but they could no longer make enough matched, genealogy-specific presentation mats for major exchanges. The established cycle of inherited cultivar stewardship, communal leaf preparation, named weaving roles, intergenerational instruction, and reciprocal presentation would cease in its current form. Retaining a narrow authorization for two supervised treatments annually in registered ceremonial gardens would sustain that practice, while continuing the lagoon’s pesticide exposure.

Should the regional government choose the pesticide-free recharge zone that protects the marine ecosystem or retain supervised imidacloprid use to protect the ceremonial practice?
Cancel authorization for imidacloprid treatment of pandanus and prohibit its use throughout the mapped limestone recharge bench.

title: Pandanus pesticide ban above a ceremonial reef lagoon

messages.content:
A public land-management authority must decide how to use a narrow river terrace between two woodland parks. Because a concrete-lined river reach, floodwall, and active rail embankment block other routes, the terrace is the only continuous shaded soil-and-vegetation connection between the parks. If the authority adopts a no-build, no-paving, and no-clearing overlay, its canopy, moist soil, leaf litter, and understory will remain intact. Woodland salamanders, ground beetles, small mammals, and understory plant propagules will continue moving between the parks, supporting recolonization and demographic and genetic exchange. The cooperative discount grocer would retain its current loading area, but could not expand its truck access or cold storage.

Approving the lease amendment would allow the grocer to pave the terrace for a larger turning and unloading yard and build a refrigerated annex. Consolidated deliveries and immediate cold storage would reduce handling and spoilage costs, supporting lower prices, a broader ordinary food range, and more reliable weekly stocking for residents of three low-income neighborhoods, many of whom lack cars and otherwise need two buses to reach another full-service grocer. Yet the construction would remove the last continuous shaded connection, leaving hot pavement, dry edges, curbs, lighting, and truck traffic that isolate the parks’ cover-dependent populations and make small local populations more vulnerable after ordinary disturbances.

Should the public land-management authority choose the corridor overlay that protects habitat connectivity or approve the expansion that protects affordable, reliable food access?

Adopt a no-build, no-paving, and no-clearing corridor overlay across the full terrace, retain its continuous canopy and understory, and revegetate only compacted terrace margins that are outside the cooperative’s currently authorized loading area.

title: Riparian corridor or discount-grocery expansion

messages.content:
An elected Indigenous governing council must decide whether to cancel a planned replacement gravity-fed slalom course beside a natural rapid in its territory. The existing council-owned course is being dismantled because its diversion wall and training structures no longer meet engineering safety standards. A replacement would provide predictable local whitewater flows for youth teams, adult clubs, families, coaches, school groups, and regional events. Without it, flat-water paddling and occasional trips to a managed course two hours away remain possible, but dependable local instruction, weekly practice, competitions, and family slalom gatherings would end for many participants.

Immediately below the rapid, several connected gravel pockets contain the entire global population of a mussel found nowhere else. If the council cancels the project, seasonal moderate flows will continue to flush fine sediment from these pockets, preserving the pore spaces the mussels need for feeding, respiration, juvenile settlement, and reproduction. If it authorizes the course, its low diversion sill and side-channel intake will reduce the velocity and bed shear of those same flows below the threshold needed to clear sediment. The gravel will repeatedly become embedded, impairing adults and preventing juvenile recruitment throughout the species’ last habitat, placing it on a trajectory toward global loss.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council cancel the replacement course to protect the endemic mussel, or build and operate it to preserve affordable, predictable local whitewater recreation?
Cancel the replacement slalom course, remove temporary project works, and leave the natural rapid and downstream reach without a new sill, intake, or training-flow diversion.

title: Cancel a replacement whitewater course to preserve an endemic river mussel

messages.content:
Across a cool-temperate estuary, naturally floating sedge marshes link an inland fen to shallow lagoons and the sea. Their living sedges and interwoven rhizomes form buoyant mats through which water, seeds, organic matter, invertebrates, amphibians, and other wetland organisms move. Licensed crews cut and roll sections of these mats for erosion-control products at a worker-owned cooperative mill in the principal town. At the minimum harvest volume needed to keep the mill open, the resulting openings align with winter waves. Unsupported edges tear, nearby gaps merge, and detached rafts strand or sink, progressively dividing the wetland chain into isolated remnants.

Under national wetland law, a national government may ban commercial removal of live sedge mats throughout the estuary for twelve years. This would allow cut edges to knit together, restore continuity across old openings, and preserve the connected functioning of the marshes. But without legal live-mat supply, the mill would close; cutting, processing, haulage, repair, dock, and storage income would disappear, buyers would turn elsewhere, and the town would lose a reliable specialized employment network for many years. Social insurance and casual work remain available, but predictable seasonal income for the cooperative and linked businesses would decline.

Should the national government choose the twelve-year harvest ban that protects wetland continuity, or continue permits at the minimum annual volume that protects local economic stability?
Ban commercial removal of live sedge mats throughout the estuary for twelve years, allowing cut edges to knit together and the floating marsh chain to expand across existing gaps.

title: Floating-Marsh Sedge Harvest Ban

messages.content:
A municipal council must decide whether to remove an obsolete irrigation dam whose crest carries the narrow public road linking two orchard villages to the valley service center and regional transport. Complete removal would drain the reservoir and restore diffuse spring flow, shallow groundwater variation, and natural salinity gradients across the valley floor. Rush meadow, saltgrass flats, greasewood margins, and seasonal wildflowers could again form a connected native plant community, with its zones able to shift as wetting patterns change. Retaining and rehabilitating the dam would leave the central habitat under deep, stable impoundment, with weeds along the reservoir edge and only narrow native fragments.

Removing the dam would also close the crest road. Residents would still reach schools, medical care, jobs, shops, emergency services, and regional transport, but the only all-season public route would add 29 kilometers and about 45 minutes each way. School and worker minibuses would make fewer daily rotations, and some early or evening trips would no longer connect with regional buses. Households would face recurring additional fuel or fare costs. Keeping the dam would preserve the direct twelve-minute route and its timed minibus connections, but would continue to prevent recovery of the valley’s native plant community.

Should the municipal council choose complete dam removal to protect the native plant community, or rehabilitate and retain the dam to protect residents’ mobility?

Completely remove the dam, spillway, and crest-road embankment; use staged drawdown to avoid burying the spring outlets; regrade only compacted construction surfaces; control reservoir-edge weeds; and use seed collected from local remnant and reference stands where natural recolonization is insufficient. The restored floor would then remain free of a replacement road so diffuse spring flow and the full wet-meadow-to-alkali-shrub zonation can recover.

title: Reservoir causeway linking orchard villages to the valley bus line

messages.content:
Four municipalities share a volcanic caldera where warm springs, supplied by a confined geothermal reservoir, sustain a mineral wetland. The springs support warm microbial mats and other primary producers, grazing snails and insect larvae, small native fish, amphibians, and resident and wintering birds that feed on wetland prey. Existing geothermal wells also supply a jointly owned district-heating network used by about 8,000 apartment residents and small shops. Four approved production wells would provide enough local heat to meet winter peak demand while maintaining current tariffs, ordinary overnight temperatures, and unrestricted hot-water service.

Pressure tests show that operating the new wells for useful winter capacity would lower reservoir pressure below the threshold that sustains every spring. Two peripheral springs would stop flowing, while remaining warm reaches would shrink. Primary-production zones and their associated prey would decline, weakening feeding links for fish and amphibians and reducing bird foraging opportunities.

The intermunicipal public authority can designate the entire recharge basin as a protected area, barring the wells and holding current withdrawals at their capped level. Essential heat and hot water would remain available, but tariffs would rise, overnight network settings would be cooler, and nonessential hot-water use would face scheduled limits during the coldest weeks. Should the intermunicipal public authority designate the protected area to preserve trophic integrity or allow the wells to protect affordable, unrestricted winter energy access?

Designate the entire mapped spring recharge basin as a protected area, prohibit the four new production wells and any other increase in geothermal withdrawal within the shared pressure compartment, and continue existing withdrawals at their current capped level.

title: Caldera wetland reserve versus expansion of a geothermal heating field

messages.content:
A subtropical river basin’s old-growth blackwater swamp forest contains veteran hollow trees, deep organic soils, accumulated deadwood, and long-established fungal and invertebrate communities. Fern farms on surrounding former swamp land operate lawfully under expiring authority leases, but their connected drains and shared outfall lower the dry-season water table along the forest’s edge. If drainage continues, exposed organic soil will keep oxidizing and subsiding, veteran trees will face repeated root stress, and dry-site species and predators will progressively displace characteristic swamp organisms from the perimeter inward.

The river-basin authority can decline to renew the leases, close the outfall, block drains, remove raised production beds, and restore a continuous swamp buffer. This would retain water, reduce damage at the old-growth margin, and allow swamp vegetation, organic-soil processes, and specialist communities to recover across the strips. It would also end commercial fern production there. Although compensation, debt settlement for eligible improvements, temporary income support, and retraining would prevent severe deprivation, growers would lose established businesses, and cutters, graders, and refrigerated-truck contractors would have to seek lower-paid or less regular work after the shared grading and transport system becomes unviable.

Alternatively, the authority can renew the leases and preserve the year-round production, floral-market contracts, grading shed, collection route, and specialized livelihoods, while leaving the forest’s edge subject to continued drawdown. Should the river-basin authority choose full restoration to protect the old-growth ecosystem or renew the leases to protect these livelihoods?

Decline renewal of the fern-farm leases, compensate documented leasehold improvements and transition costs, close the shared drainage outfall, block field drains, grade down raised production beds, and establish locally sourced swamp trees and appropriate ground-layer vegetation as a continuous wet buffer around the old-growth core.

title: Rewetting Plantation Strips Around an Ancient Swamp Forest

messages.content:
A state or provincial natural-resources agency operates a headwater reservoir that supplies a permitted early-winter snowmaking diversion to a privately owned ski area and releases water to an alpine stream inhabited by native sculpin. Upstream and downstream breeding groups carry different cold-metabolism and disease-resistance variants. During recurring low-inflow periods, the fish can move between winter refuges and contribute to breeding only if reservoir releases keep shallow riffles above a measured under-ice depth threshold. Reserving enough water for continuous passage would maintain gene flow and reduce the loss of these distinct variants through drift and inbreeding.

That reservation would reduce the ski area’s historical snowmaking allocation during its narrow early freezing window. It would leave insufficient water to establish a durable base on much of the developed lower-elevation terrain, causing delayed or intermittent closures and reducing lift revenue, concession rent, equipment use, and the income and resale value tied to its lifts, graded runs, pipelines, pumps, and snowmaking plant. The resort could still operate higher natural-snow terrain. Granting the historical allocation, however, would preserve ordinary use and value of those specialized facilities while allowing the riffles to become repeatedly impassable, isolating the smaller upstream group and making its rare variants progressively more likely to disappear, even though the species would remain in the watershed. Should the agency reserve water for winter stream connectivity or allocate it to protect the ski area’s property use?
Reserve enough stored water for continuous winter stream discharge above the measured riffle-connectivity threshold, reducing the ski area’s early-winter snowmaking allocation.

title: Winter headwater flow versus snowmaking property use

messages.content:
A reservoir-regulated river narrows between reed shelves that become too shallow for large fish during scheduled drawdowns. Twenty-seven lawfully licensed houseboats, occupied as primary homes, stand in two offset rows across most of the only channel that remains adequately deep year-round. Their piles, cross-channel utility lines, illuminated gangways, and routine maneuvering leave migratory eels, lampreys, and barbel with only narrow, brightly lit passages. As a result, movement between downstream feeding and overwintering habitat and upstream spawning or maturation reaches remains too low to prevent demographic isolation.

The houseboats also form a settled neighborhood. Residents share childcare, meals, repairs, transport, and daily assistance for older people. The river-basin authority may designate the narrows as a protected aquatic migration corridor, remove the infrastructure, and relocate every vessel to licensed downstream basins. This would restore a continuous, dark, deep route for fish, but would compel all households to leave their present homes. Although the authority would provide replacement berths and pay relocation-related costs, no single basin can hold all twenty-seven vessels, so the community would be divided among three sites.

Alternatively, the authority can exclude the narrows from protection and renew the mooring licences, allowing residents to remain in their homes and preserve their community, while the only year-round deep migration route remains obstructed. Should the river-basin authority designate the protected corridor or renew the licences to protect the residents’ continued homes and community?

Designate the narrows as a protected aquatic migration corridor, prohibit permanent residential moorings and fixed cross-channel utilities within it, remove the piles and chains, extinguish the mooring-field lighting, and relocate the houseboats to licensed downstream basins.

title: Relocating a houseboat community from a deep migration channel

messages.content:
An elected Indigenous governing council must decide whether to remove the concrete diversion weir serving its community’s run-of-river power plant. The Pali stream goby exists nowhere beyond the island’s eastern watershed. Its juveniles must climb from the estuary to cool upper tributaries, but the weir’s smooth face and concrete apron block most of them, while diversion dries the bypassed reach’s climbing margins during migration. If the council removes the weir, intake apron, and armoring, a continuously wetted rough channel will reconnect the estuary to all three upper tributaries. The goby’s breeding groups will again exchange individuals across most of its range. If the weir remains, two upper breeding groups will disappear locally, leaving the species confined to one warmer, more disturbed lower-stream area.

The plant supplies about one-third of the electricity used by 1,300 residents and several family workshops. Removing the weir ends that generation. Imported-diesel backup will preserve clinic service, basic lighting and cooking, minimum refrigeration, and enough power to avoid dangerous deprivation, but tariffs will rise persistently. Residents will face scheduled nonessential evening curtailments, workshops will shorten shifts, and communal cold storage will be available only in assigned time slots. Retaining the weir preserves current tariffs, ordinary evening electricity, unrestricted refrigeration schedules, and workshop hours.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council remove the weir to protect the endemic Pali stream goby or retain it to protect the community’s affordable, reliable energy access?
Remove the diversion weir, intake apron, and armoring along the bypassed reach, then stabilize the disturbed banks without installing another channel-spanning barrier.

title: Removing the Intake Weir for the Pali Stream Goby

messages.content:
Four municipalities share a warm limestone coast where submerged caves, entrances, and shaded ledges form a connected marine district. Licensed divers lawfully collect natural sponges under concessions issued by the intermunicipal marine-commons authority. The largest, slow-growing sponge colonies filter water, process nutrients, and create cavities and irregular refuge for crustaceans, juvenile groupers, worms, and colonial invertebrates. Because harvest has removed large marketable colonies faster than comparable colonies can mature, cleared walls remain dominated by short-lived mats and small recruits. Filtration and structural refuge remain depressed, and cave-community assemblages are sparse and fragmented across connected entrances and ledges.
