Five years of monitoring under successively reduced quotas showed that any commercially meaningful harvest remained concentrated on the same mature colonies, with removals still exceeding their replacement, while rotating entrances allowed reopened sectors to be harvested before mature structure and connectivity returned. The authority can therefore either impose a fourteen-year ban on commercial and personal sponge harvest throughout the district or continue licensed cutting under the current quota. A ban would allow large colonies to survive through multiple maturation and recruitment cycles, reconnecting habitat and supporting a more complex marine community. It would also leave the cooperative of licensed divers with no legal crop from its concessions for fourteen years. Their purpose-built curing house would lose its ordinary function, and their specialized boats, compressors, concessions, supplemental income, and retirement assets would lose substantial value, although compensation and other income protect housing and basic needs. Continuing the quota would preserve the productive use, transfer value, and seasonal returns of those lawful holdings, while mature sponge habitat, filtration, and refuge would remain reduced. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose the fourteen-year harvest ban to protect the marine ecosystem or continue licensed harvesting to protect the cooperative’s property interests?
Ban commercial and personal sponge harvest throughout the submerged-cave district for fourteen years, allowing several uninterrupted growth and recruitment cycles.

title: Sponge-harvest closure in a submerged cave district

messages.content:
During a forecast two-season locust outbreak in a semi-arid inland district, bands move repeatedly between rain-fed millet fields and openings in a large, long-continuous dry forest. The regional environmental regulatory agency must decide whether to deny broad-spectrum aerial spraying across the field–forest mosaic, including forest edges and internal openings. That choice would prevent spray deposition and drift into the old-growth ecosystem, preserving seasonal insect abundance and the pollination, decomposition, aquatic emergence, prey, and nutrient-transfer relationships that connect ancient trees, deadwood, termite mounds, seasonal pools, birds, bats, and reptiles.

Without synchronized aerial treatment across the full outbreak area, locusts sheltering in forest openings will return to adjacent millet during grain filling. Two consecutive saleable harvests will be substantially reduced, along with retained seed and household grain reserves. Trucked maize and other grains will prevent acute hunger, but limited transport and storage capacity will leave low-income households in six market towns facing elevated meal prices, recurring shop stock gaps, less dietary variety, and pressure on ordinary household and school food budgets. A partial campaign would still expose forest margins to drift while failing to protect enough millet for local mills and markets.

Should the environmental regulatory agency choose to protect the old-growth ecosystem or to protect reliable, affordable food access for the six towns?

Deny authorization for broad-spectrum aerial locust spraying across the field–forest mosaic, including forest edges and internal openings, thereby preventing direct spray deposition and drift into the old-growth ecosystem.

title: Locust-control restriction around an ancient dry-forest mosaic

messages.content:
On a windy oceanic headland, separate cliff colonies of wild perennial brassica carry distinct combinations of flowering-time, salt-spray-tolerance, and drought-response variants. Nearby farms have lawfully grown commercial flowering brassica seed, but bees carry crop pollen across the measured four-kilometre range. Repeated hybridization and backcrossing introduce the same abundant commercial alleles into every colony. If this continues, the wild plants will remain, yet rare local variants and the genetic differences among the cliff lineages will progressively decline.

A regional planning commission can adopt a continuing overlay that prohibits commercial flowering brassica seed crops within four kilometres of each wild colony, while allowing unrelated crops and brassicas harvested before flowering. This would reduce crop-pollen input enough for the colonies to retain their distinctive genetic variation. But the three seed-growing households would lose premium seed contracts, seasonal field positions would disappear, and the cleaning and certification cooperative would fall below the volume needed to cover its costs. The households could keep their land, grow lower-margin crops, and receive conversion grants, but their specialist income would decline markedly and the established cooperative operation would become nonviable.

If the commission declines the restriction, the farms’ contracted rotations, specialist work, seasonal employment, certification throughput, and associated income will continue, while the headland’s wild lineages become increasingly genetically homogenized. Should the regional planning commission adopt the ecologically protective overlay or preserve the established seed-growing livelihood?

Adopt a continuing agricultural-use overlay prohibiting commercial flowering brassica seed crops within four kilometres of every wild colony. Unrelated crops and brassicas harvested before flowering remain permitted.

title: Flowering-crop buffer around wild coastal brassicas

messages.content:
A public land-management authority must decide whether to cancel a planned concrete-lined flood-bypass channel and maintenance road across a desert conservation estate. The channel’s only hydraulically workable alignment crosses the estate’s sole broad remnant of a native alluvial-fan plant community: a contiguous mosaic of saltbush, bursage, native grasses, and ephemeral wildflowers. If the project is cancelled, diffuse fan flows will continue to shift among distributaries, sorting sediment, redistributing seeds, and creating the changing moisture conditions that sustain this plant community. If it is built, it will permanently capture principal distributary flows, dry downslope patches, concentrate scour and deposition along its margins, and divide the community with a channel, road, and persistent invasive-plant edges.

The bypass would also keep recurring shallow fan flows out of a forty-home village, preserving residents’ homes, long-held plots, shared courtyards, nearby relatives, and neighborhood continuity. Without it, the authority must acquire the parcels before the safety-compliance deadline, relocate households to comparable serviced homes in the adjacent town, provide compensation and moving assistance, and remove the village infrastructure. Residents would be safe and housed, but would be compelled to leave their established community. Smaller structures, alternative routes, and household floodproofing cannot meet the required safety standard while keeping the village’s shared road, drainage, and septic system functional.

Should the public land-management authority cancel the bypass to protect the native plant community, or construct it to protect residents’ ability to remain in their homes?

Cancel the bypass channel and maintenance road, acquire the village parcels, relocate residents before the safety-compliance deadline, remove the acquired buildings and residential infrastructure, and restore disturbed ground so diffuse fan flows can again cross the lower fan.

title: Cancel the flood-bypass channel or retain homes in an alluvial-fan village

messages.content:
A regional electric railway crosses a basalt ridge through an aging tunnel beneath a perched aquifer. For the next eight years, the regional government must decide whether to reserve the aquifer’s limited dry-season yield for the wooded valley’s spring runs or renew pumping that keeps the tunnel safe for normal rail service. Reserving the water would maintain continuous flow, oxygenated riffles, and connected pools. Periphyton and leaf litter would sustain grazing and shredding insects; those insects would support minnows and salamanders, and aquatic insects and vertebrate prey would sustain kingfishers, water snakes, and other riparian predators. Pumping at the established rate would intercept most dry-season recharge, causing several spring runs to stop flowing and weakening these food-web relationships.

Without dewatering, hydrostatic pressure would exceed the tunnel lining’s certified limit, requiring its closure. Safe replacement buses would still connect the three outer suburbs to work, education, medical appointments, caregiving, and family visits, but the winding ridge-road trips would add 45–70 minutes each way, run less often in the evening, require additional transfers, and lack train capacity during peak periods. Renewing pumping would preserve frequent through-trains, affordable predictable travel times, and convenient connections, particularly for households without routine access to a car. Pumping below the operational rate would still leave tunnel pressure above the certified limit while withdrawing enough water to stop flow in the smallest spring runs.

Should the regional government reserve the aquifer for the spring-run food web or renew tunnel pumping to protect residents’ mobility?
End the tunnel's groundwater-withdrawal permit for the eight-year allocation period and reserve the perched aquifer's dry-season yield for continuous discharge through the valley spring runs.

title: Aquifer reserve or drainage of a regional rail tunnel

messages.content:
A state or provincial natural-resources agency must decide whether to renew the expiring lease of a worker cooperative operating the central ponds of a provincially owned saltworks estate. The estate lies between two remnant tidal marshes, and its levees, pumps, and truck causeways occupy the only low-elevation route connecting them to each other and to the estuary. If the agency declines renewal, it can breach levees, remove pumps and obstructing causeway sections, regrade the pond floors, excavate tidal creeks, and establish salt-marsh vegetation. Tides would then reconnect tidal creek, mudflat, salt marsh, and shallow lagoon habitats, carrying sediment, detritus, fish, invertebrates, and plant propagules through the former pond system.

Renewal would preserve the hydraulically isolated ponds required for commercial salt production. The cooperative would retain its contract-grade output, year-round workforce, buyer relationships, trucking activity, and the local spending that supports freight, repair, retail, and municipal revenue in a small town where it is the principal private employer. Restoration would end that production because the complete linked pond sequence is necessary to concentrate brine. Although transition funding, unemployment support, road access, and regional employment opportunities would prevent destitution or displacement, the town would face prolonged losses of specialized jobs, income, and interconnected business activity.

Should the agency choose habitat restoration that protects wetland continuity, or renew the lease to protect local economic stability?

Decline lease renewal at the scheduled expiration, breach the seaward and cross-pond levees, remove pumps and obstructing causeway sections, regrade concentration and crystallizer floors, excavate branching tidal creeks, and establish locally sourced salt-marsh vegetation across the former pond train.

title: Restoring tidal continuity through a working salt landscape

messages.content:
A city-owned rocky foreshore contains the municipality’s only safely accessible tidepooling shore. For decades, families, school-age nature clubs, older naturalists, and residents without reliable private transport have used its intertidal pools for close observation, photography, species identification, and hands-on natural-history learning. The municipal council can either retain managed low-tide entry with visitor limits, designated access periods, and bans on collecting or handling organisms, or designate the entire platform a marine protected area and prohibit entry onto the rock for twelve years. Coastal walking and cliff-top viewing would remain available under closure, but users would lose access to the pools themselves, and distant shores are not a practical replacement for regular local outings.

Visitors must cross the central mussel and algal bands along a few gently sloped safe routes. Repeated foot placement crushes mussel and snail recruits and dislodges canopy algae, leaving bare corridors that become hotter and drier at low tide. These corridors fragment mussel beds, shaded crevices, and pool-edge cover, preventing recovery of grazers, filter feeders, predators, crustaceans, and juvenile fish that use the reef as an interacting community. Five years of capped access, walking lines, and monitoring did not stop the damage. A twelve-year closure would allow mussels and canopy algae to regain continuous cover and reconnect the moisture-retaining habitat on which the community depends.

Should the municipal council choose the protected-area closure that restores the marine ecosystem or managed access that preserves regular hands-on tidepool recreation?

Designate the entire reef platform as a marine protected area and prohibit entry onto the intertidal rock for twelve years, while retaining access to the landward cliff path and viewing points. Twelve years is the surveyed period needed for mussel cohorts and canopy algae to re-establish continuous cover across the damaged corridors under local recruitment rates.

title: Closure of a trampling-sensitive intertidal reef platform

messages.content:
A nationally owned barrier island contains a degraded dune neck separating the only two surviving patches of an island-endemic burrowing skink. The neck is the only terrain that can be restored into connected loose-sand habitat. Tamarisk windbreaks, a stone platform and stabilizing apron, and compacted ceremonial approaches now hold the sand in place. Removing them, recontouring the area, and restoring sparse native dune cover would allow wind to move sand through the neck again, reconnecting feeding, breeding, shelter, and dispersal habitat across most of the skink’s remaining potential range.

The stone platform is also the inherited setting for a midsummer signal-fire ceremony shared by five coastal communities. Families carry embers from their household hearths, light a large beacon, exchange songs with answering fires visible across the strait, and return the fire to their community halls. The rite renews shared ancestry and reciprocal obligations. Restoring the dune would prohibit the gathering and large fire, ending the unified, place-based ceremony; songs and separate local fires could continue, but not the reciprocal beacon sequence. Retaining the platform, windbreaks, hardened access, and fire-control clearing would preserve the ceremony but leave the skink patches small and isolated, with little movement through the neck.

Should the national government choose dune restoration to protect the endemic skink or retain the site to protect the communities’ cultural practice?

Remove the tamarisk windbreaks, dismantle the platform's stabilizing apron, loosen and recontour compacted approaches, restore wind-scoured sand movement, establish sparse locally native dune vegetation, and prohibit the beacon gathering and large fire within the restored neck.

title: Dune restoration at an ancestral signal-fire ground

messages.content:
In a temperate lake basin, twelve family orchard owners operate mature apple and pear parcels on the lower terraces of six tributaries. Their post-bloom insecticide applications are carried by scheduled irrigation into subsurface tile drains, producing repeated pulses in the tributaries that are lethal to sensitive mayfly, stonefly, and caddisfly larvae. These insects are a seasonal food source for juvenile native fish, and their emergence supports feeding by bats and nesting swallows. If the pulses continue, the tributary network remains dominated by tolerant organisms, with weakened links among aquatic insects, fish, and aerial insectivores.

The river-basin authority can prohibit the insecticide in the mapped source area for nine years, allowing aquatic-insect and fish cohorts to recover. But without it, internal pest damage exceeds fresh-market buyer tolerances. Transition grants would prevent foreclosure and support debt restructuring and gradual replanting, yet the owners would lose years of ordinary orchard income, much of the productive value of mature trees, and part of their equity in the jointly owned grading and cold-storage facility.

Alternatively, the authority can renew licensed applications at existing rates and setbacks. The orchards would retain saleable yields, and the mature trees, parcels, and specialized facility would preserve their established agricultural and collateral value, while the tributary food web would remain impaired. Should the river-basin authority choose the prohibition that protects trophic integrity or renew the pesticide use that protects the orchard owners’ property?

Prohibit use of the insecticide throughout the mapped source area for nine years. This period covers establishment of replacement orchard blocks and allows multiple aquatic-insect and native-fish cohorts to recover under continued monitoring.

title: Mayfly-safe insecticide rule for an orchard tributary belt

messages.content:
A regional government must decide whether to cancel a planned extension of the airport runway serving a roadless subarctic settlement. The extension would add a freight apron, approach-light corridor, and wildlife-exclusion fence across the only broad, low-gradient passage between coastal caribou calving grounds and inland winter range. Steep broken ground and thaw-sensitive wetlands constrain movement around it. If the project is cancelled, the existing short, unfenced gravel runway will remain in use, leaving the passage open for caribou to migrate, disperse, mix between regional groups, and recolonize areas after difficult winters.

If the government authorizes construction, larger cargo aircraft will be able to carry substantially greater refrigerated and palletized freight throughout the year. Stores will restock weekly, recurring gaps in produce, eggs, dairy, and other ordinary foods will decline, and lower freight costs will reduce prices. Without the extension, households—especially low- and moderate-income families—will continue facing high food prices, limited variety, less frequent refrigerated deliveries, and multi-day gaps in fresh foods, though subsidies, reserve stocks, and emergency flights will preserve adequate nutrition.

Should the regional government cancel the runway extension to protect habitat connectivity for caribou, or construct it to improve reliable, affordable food access for settlement households?

Cancel the runway extension, freight apron, approach-light corridor, and new perimeter fence while continuing to operate the existing short, unfenced runway. This leaves the full width of the established passage available to moving caribou.

title: Cancel a tundra cargo-runway extension across a caribou passage

messages.content:
An environmental regulatory agency must decide whether to renew the operating permissions for an old navigation dam retrofitted with hydropower turbines in a postindustrial river district. The dam divides three surviving beds of native river mussels. Their larvae disperse only while attached to migratory redhorse fish, but the dam and its eight-kilometre deep, slow, fine-sediment reservoir prevent the fish from moving effectively among the reaches and eliminate the flowing-shoal habitat needed for mussel recruitment. Each bed contains uncommon alleles associated with shell strength, temperature tolerance, and parasite resistance. If the dam remains, the beds will stay isolated, and drift and inbreeding will progressively reduce regional genetic diversity.

The agency may deny renewal and require removal of the dam, navigation sill, turbines, and sediment plug, restoring a free-flowing channel. Redhorse would then again carry larvae among all three beds, maintaining gene exchange and those uncommon traits in a connected mussel population. Yet removal would permanently end the public utility’s low-cost power allocation. Under its established replacement contract, household bills would rise materially and persistently; food processors would stagger operations away from costly evening periods, while public charging sites and repair workshops would reduce evening hours. Essential electricity, safe heating, and food-safety refrigeration would remain available.

Should the environmental regulatory agency require dam removal to protect genetic diversity or renew the permissions to protect affordable, predictable energy access?

Refuse renewal of the facility's operating permissions and require removal of the dam, navigation sill, turbines, and accumulated fine-sediment plug, followed by stabilization of released sediment and restoration of a free-flowing channel.

title: Removing an industrial-river hydropower dam to reconnect native mussel breeding beds

messages.content:
A public land-management authority must decide whether to impose a twelve-year ban on taking clams and other burrowing shellfish from a centuries-continuous eelgrass meadow in an estuarine reserve. The meadow’s interwoven rhizome mat, shell deposits, tidal microchannels, sediment gradients, and patch-specific benthic communities are mature structures that cannot be recreated quickly. Continued hand-digging, even under current bag limits, approved tools, and hole-filling rules, creates pits and cuts rhizomes. Winter waves enlarge nearby pits into erosional gaps, fragmenting the connected meadow mosaic. With twelve undisturbed years, scars can regain the mature meadow’s rhizome density, elevation, and benthic assemblages.

The ban would stop new digging damage while retaining boardwalk viewing, shoreline access, and non-harvest observation. Yet it would prohibit entry onto the vegetated flat for digging, removing the only nearby, firm, safely walkable public clam-harvesting ground for residents of three coastal towns. Older adults and families regularly use the site to dig clams, teach harvesting skills, and prepare shared weekend meals. Other flats are dangerously soft or require private boats, so they are not practical alternatives for many users. Renewing permits would preserve this frequent, affordable, intergenerational recreation but allow the meadow’s fragmentation to continue.

Should the public land-management authority choose the twelve-year harvest ban to protect the old-growth ecosystem, or renew permits to protect residents’ recreational clam-digging?

Impose a twelve-year ban on taking clams and other burrowing shellfish throughout the old-growth eelgrass meadow. Boardwalk viewing, shoreline access, and non-harvest observation remain allowed, but entry onto the vegetated intertidal flat for digging is prohibited.

title: Clam-harvest ban in a long-continuous eelgrass meadow

messages.content:
Five towns share a river delta whose seasonally flooded clay meadows form the only continuous low-elevation transition between inland reed marshes and brackish coastal wetlands. As existing clay-extraction permits near expiry, an intermunicipal public authority must decide whether to designate this corridor a no-extraction zone or renew phased extraction permissions for twenty years.

Prohibiting further pits, dewatering ditches, spoil bunds, and haul roads would retain the continuous band of shallow-flooded meadow. Its moisture and salinity gradient would continue to sustain characteristic meadow plant zonation and the movement of insects, amphibians, floodplain fish during inundation, seeds, detritus, and fine sediment among the wetland zones. But when permits expire, local clay extraction would end. Two roof-tile kilns would lose the clay blend required by their equipment and certified products, and linked digging, haulage, finishing, and sales firms would lose recurring work. Grants and employment assistance would limit material hardship, yet specialized careers, family-firm income, productive assets, and business value would be lost.

Renewing extraction would preserve the established tile-production cluster, skilled jobs, contracts, and family businesses for twenty years. Successive pits and their required drainage and road structures, however, would replace the continuous seasonal meadow gradient with deep permanent ponds and dry barriers, disrupting wet-meadow habitat and lateral flow between the inland and coastal wetlands. Should the intermunicipal public authority choose the no-extraction zone that protects wetland continuity or renew extraction to protect local livelihoods?

Designate the wet-meadow corridor as a no-extraction land-use zone, deny renewal of expiring clay permits, prohibit new pits, dewatering ditches, spoil bunds, and haul roads, and restore disturbed parcel edges where the original meadow substrate remains.

title: Clay-extraction prohibition in a delta wet-meadow corridor

messages.content:
Each summer, a municipal council must assign the fixed output of its tertiary-treatment plant. The available reclaimed water can either be sent through subsurface infiltration basins to a protected dune field or used to irrigate a long-established neighborhood garden. Supplying the monitored minimum volume to the dunes would maintain the shallow seasonal groundwater range that sustains their native sedges, rushes, orchids, mint, and annual wetland herbs. The slacks would retain their alternating wet and moist zones, allowing orchids and wetland annuals to flower and recruit rather than giving way to dry scrub and invasive grasses.

The same allocation would end summer deliveries to the garden used by several hundred families for a four-generation diaspora New Year practice. Reliable irrigation presently permits coordinated planting and watering, teaching in the fields, cultivation of selected herbs and vegetables, seed saving and exchange, and a collective harvest. Families could still obtain food, meet, cook shared recipes, and observe the New Year date, but purchased produce would not preserve the shared growing and harvest cycle or the locally maintained seed lines. The water supply cannot meet both minimum needs: a split would cause the dune community’s central recruitment zone and the garden’s long-season crops and seed crop to fail.

Should the municipal council allocate the water to protect the native dune-slack plant community or to protect the garden-based cultural practice?

Allocate the monitored minimum summer volume to the dune infiltration basins, maintaining the seasonal groundwater range required by the native slack community, and discontinue summer reclaimed-water deliveries to the garden.

title: Reclaimed water for dune slacks or festival gardens

messages.content:
A silty temperate embayment supports connected eelgrass beds, shell beds, benthic invertebrates, juvenile fish, and their predators. Two passenger-and-vehicle ferries berth there and repeatedly cross shallow nursery waters while serving inhabited islands. Monitoring identifies their copper-antifouling hull coatings as the principal controllable source of chronic copper exposure around the terminals and sailing corridor. If a provincial natural-resources agency denies renewal of the coatings’ permit, new copper loading will fall below the locally established effects level. Amphipods, juvenile bivalves, and eelgrass-surface grazers will recover, strengthening filtration, grazing, decomposition, and fish-prey relationships throughout the embayment’s connected community.

The restriction would require both ferries to use a nonbiocidal barrier coating and undergo repeated mechanical cleaning at a mainland yard during the roughly four-month high-fouling season. Staggered withdrawals and weather-related yard delays would reduce service from hourly departures to roughly every three hours on recurring days for eight years. Island residents—including commuters, students, patients attending routine appointments, caregivers, and tradespeople—would still have ferry service, but would face reservations, constrained vehicle capacity, missed connections, and longer routine trips. Renewing the permit would preserve hourly departures and current capacity, but copper exposure would continue to suppress sensitive invertebrates and leave eelgrass-edge and shell-bed communities simplified across a substantial part of the embayment.

Should the provincial natural-resources agency deny the permit to protect the marine ecosystem or renew it to protect island residents’ mobility?

Deny renewal of the copper-antifouling permit for both ferries. Require an abrasion-resistant, nonbiocidal epoxy barrier coating and scheduled mechanical removal of fouling at an equipped mainland yard.

title: Copper-antifouling restriction for an island passenger ferry

messages.content:
An elected Indigenous governing council must decide whether to renew commercial licences for mature native rattan in a tropical upland’s mapped gorge-and-gap network. At a limited number of bottlenecks, long rattan canes are the only continuous routes between old-forest sections. If the council imposes a nine-year harvest ban, the existing living bridges will remain intact and younger canes will grow into additional crossings. Ground-averse arboreal mammals and lizards, as well as canopy-associated invertebrates that use the stems, will continue to disperse between breeding areas and recolonize forest patches after cyclone damage.

Renewing licences at the minimum volume needed by the shared workshop would require cutting the mature canes at those bottlenecks. The resulting openings exceed the focal animals’ crossing ability, reducing movement and post-storm recolonization and fragmenting previously connected populations into smaller habitat units. Yet a ban would also remove the workshop’s only local supply of furniture-grade cane. The workshop would close, skilled cutting and craft jobs would disappear, freight contracts would lapse, and retail trade would contract in both villages. Households would retain necessities through mixed livelihoods and transition payments, but not the trade’s skilled work, business value, or predictable cash income.

Should the elected Indigenous governing council choose the nine-year harvest ban that protects habitat connectivity or renew the licences that protect local economic stability?

Ban commercial harvesting of mature native rattan throughout the mapped gorge-and-gap network for nine years. Existing spanning canes must remain intact, and younger canes must be allowed to grow to crossing length before harvesting can be reconsidered.

title: Rattan bridges across a monsoon-forest gorge network

messages.content:
A national government must decide whether to remove a nationally owned hydropower dam in a mountain watershed. The dam’s reservoir inundates the principal waterfall gorge of the silver-thread caddisfly, which exists nowhere else. Only two small tributary spray patches still support the species. Removing the dam and permanently draining the reservoir would restore free flow, waterfalls, cold spray-wetted boulder faces, and continuous habitat through the gorge. This would reconnect the surviving populations and restore a substantial part of the caddisfly’s endemic range. Retaining the dam would leave the gorge submerged, keeping the species confined to isolated spray patches that shrink during dry years.

Twenty-six lawful owner and tenant households live on an ancient landslide bench beside the reservoir. Reservoir water stabilizes the submerged toe of the slide; permanent drawdown would cause progressive ground displacement that their homes, roads, water lines, and sewers cannot withstand. If the dam is removed, residents would receive secure replacement homes, moving expenses, and tenure protection in the same municipality before any movement occurs. Yet they would have to leave their current homes and compact neighborhood, losing direct proximity to the chapel and community hall and some established daily care and maintenance relationships. Retaining the dam would allow them to remain safely in their homes and preserve their neighborhood’s routines and support network.

Should the national government remove the dam to restore the endemic caddisfly’s habitat, or retain it so the households can remain in their current community?
Remove the dam and associated powerworks, permanently drain the impoundment, and restore free flow through the gorge so its waterfalls, turbulent boulder faces, and cold spray zones re-form.

title: Drawdown of a mountain gorge reservoir above a slide-bench village

messages.content:
A storm destroyed the pedestrian pier linking a mainland public park to an offshore surf headland. The regional planning commission must decide whether to approve a continuous rock causeway with an elevated pedestrian deck or deny the authorizations required for construction. The causeway’s landing and storm-resistant abutment would occupy the headland’s only intact low dune neck, where foredune, wet-swale, and salt-spray populations of a native beach grass contain distinct genetic traits. Construction would remove most of the wet-swale breeding population and its seed bank, block storm overwash, and progressively dry and narrow the swale. Alleles concentrated in the wet-swale lineage, including waterlogging-response variants, would be lost, substantially reducing the species’ genetic breadth at the site.

Cancelling the project would leave the dune neck’s wind-driven sand movement and overwash intact, retaining the three populations and their differing burial, waterlogging, and salt tolerances. But the former pier cannot be repaired, and most members of two established surf clubs cannot safely cross the deep, current-swept channel while carrying boards. Without the causeway, youth instruction, older participants’ sessions, winter surfing, and spontaneous low-cost use of the sheltered break would largely end. Calm-weather boat trips and other beaches would remain available, but would not provide regular access for these activities.

Should the regional planning commission cancel the causeway to protect the beach grass’s genetic diversity, or approve it to restore dependable recreation for the surf clubs?
Cancel the planned causeway and elevated walkway, remove only the unsafe remains of the old pier from outside the dune neck, and leave the neck’s overwash and wind-driven sand movement intact.

title: Cancel an all-weather access causeway to a remote surf headland
